title: The jet that ran out of fuel because of one unit
hook: In 1983 a jet with 69 people ran out of fuel in midair.
summary: Air Canada Flight 143 was fuelled using pounds instead of kilograms, lost both engines over Manitoba, and glided to a safe landing at Gimli thanks to a glider-pilot captain.
sources: Wikipedia / Transport Canada inquiry: Air Canada Flight 143 (Gimli Glider), 23 July 1983, Boeing 767, 69 people aboard, all survived

Fuel loaded in pounds instead of kilograms during Canada's metric changeover; Captain Robert Pearson was an experienced glider pilot; landed at former RCAF Gimli base then used as a racetrack; nose gear collapsed; aircraft retired 2008

lines.text: In nineteen eighty-three, a jet carrying sixty-nine people ran out of fuel.
lines.caps: In *1983, | a *jet carrying | *69 people | ran out of *fuel

lines.text: Canada was switching to metric, and the fuel was counted in pounds, not kilograms.
lines.caps: Canada was *switching | to *metric, | fuel counted in *pounds, | not *kilograms

lines.text: A pound is under half a kilogram, so the tanks were far too empty.
lines.caps: A *pound | is under *half | a *kilogram, | so the *tanks | were too *empty

lines.text: Over Manitoba, both engines went silent.
The captain, Robert Pearson, happened to fly gliders.
He steered for an old air base at Gimli, now a racetrack.
lines.caps: He steered for *Gimli, | an old *air base, | now a *racetrack

lines.text: The jet landed, the nose wheel folded, and everyone lived.
lines.caps: The jet *landed, | the nose wheel *folded, | and everyone *lived

lines.text: It flew again until two thousand eight.

post.caption:
One wrong unit nearly brought down a brand new jet, and a glider pilot saved everyone.
Would you have trusted the fuel gauge?
